UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                   ​
​
​
 Docket No. ER26-3515-000 
 
 
MOTION TO INTERVENE AND COMMENTS OF SUNRUN INC. 
Pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”), 18 C.F.R. sections 385.211 and 385.214 
(2026), Sunrun Inc. (“Sunrun”) respectfully submits this Motion to Intervene and Comments 
in the above-captioned proceeding. This filing responds to the proposal by PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) 
and a Large Load Registry, filed on August 13, 2026 under Section 205 of the Federal Power 
Act, 16 U.S.C. section 824d, Accession No. 20260813-5118, with a requested effective date 
of October 12, 2026. 
Communications regarding this filing should be directed to: 
S. Becca Smith 
Sr. Assistant General Counsel 
Sunrun Inc. 
202.689.5882 
becca.smith@sunrun.com 
September 3, 2026

I. Introduction and Summary 
Pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 
18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211, 385.214 (2026), Sunrun Inc. (“Sunrun”) respectfully moves to 
intervene and submits these comments in the above-captioned proceeding. On August 13, 
2026, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) filed proposed tariff revisions under Section 205 
of the Federal Power Act to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) and a 
Large Load Registry. Accession No. 20260813-5118. PJM requests an effective date of 
October 12, 2026. 
Sunrun is the nation’s largest residential solar and battery storage company and 
operates as a distributed energy resource (“DER”) aggregator serving customers across 
multiple PJM transmission zones. PJM’s proposed treatment of DERs, aggregation rules, and 
IRAS compliance obligations directly affects Sunrun’s market participation and its 
customers’ interests. 
Sunrun’s comments address five substantive issues: (1) verified Peak Shaving 
Adjustment (“PSA”) megawatts under qualifying state programs should offset IRAS 
obligations on a megawatt-for-megawatt basis; (2) battery storage injections must be settled 
separately from net-metered solar exports through device-level submetering; (3) residential 
DERs require broader multi-nodal aggregation across electric distribution company service 
territories or transmission zones; (4) PJM’s existing registration process requires transparency 
and accountability measures to address uneven state and EDC readiness; and (5) routine 
portfolio additions and like-for-like substitutions should receive expedited, ministerial 
treatment rather than retriggering full review or being barred during a Delivery Year. 
Sunrun respectfully requests that the Commission accept PJM’s filing subject to a 
discrete clarification or compliance filing confirming that verified PSA values reduce IRAS

obligations, with appropriate measurement, verification, performance scoring, reconciliation, 
and no-double-counting safeguards, or, in the alternative, reject the filing without prejudice. 
For the remaining DER implementation issues, Sunrun requests that the Commission convene 
a technical conference or direct a coordinated follow-up proceeding. 
II. Motion to Intervene 
Pursuant to Rules 211 and 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 
18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211 and 385.214 (2026), Sunrun Inc. (“Sunrun”) respectfully moves to 
intervene in the above-captioned proceeding. 
Sunrun is a leading provider of residential solar energy and battery storage systems 
and operates as a distributed energy resource (“DER”) aggregator. Sunrun maintains 
customers and direct market interests across multiple PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) 
territories. Based on a recent bilateral partnership, Sunrun plans to participate in wholesale 
markets and programs administered by PJM and is directly affected by PJM's tariff provisions 
governing DER participation, aggregation, and resource adequacy.   
PJM’s August 13, 2026 filing in this docket proposes to establish an Interim Resource 
Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) and a Large Load Registry. The proposed tariff revisions, 
including the treatment of DERs, aggregation rules, Peak Shaving Adjustments, and IRAS 
compliance obligations, directly affect Sunrun’s ability to participate in PJM markets and to 
serve its customers. The outcome of this proceeding will shape the terms under which 
Sunrun’s DER fleet can contribute to resource adequacy and the conditions under which 
Sunrun’s customers may benefit from or be burdened by IRAS-related requirements. 
Sunrun’s intervention is in the public interest. Sunrun will bring the perspective of a 
residential DER provider and aggregator that no other party is positioned to represent with

the same specificity. No existing party’s interest will be prejudiced by Sunrun’s participation, 
and Sunrun’s intervention will assist the Commission in developing a complete record. 
Sunrun respectfully requests that the Commission grant this motion. 
III. Comments 
Sunrun respectfully submits the following comments on PJM’s August 13, 2026 
Section 205 filing proposing Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry. 
These comments address six related subjects, organized in Sections III.A through III.F below. 
One request is appropriately resolved within the Section 205 standard of review: 
PJM’s filed tariff and registry already collect each Large Load’s Peak Shaving Adjustment 
value under a qualifying state program, yet the filing does not specify how verified PSA 
megawatts reduce a Large Load’s IRAS obligation. The Commission can and should direct a 
discrete clarification or compliance filing on that point, consistent with the principle that a 
utility’s Section 205 filing must be just and reasonable in its own terms. See 16 U.S.C. 
section 824d(a). If PJM cannot demonstrate that its proposal adequately accounts for verified 
PSA values, the Commission should reject the filing without prejudice to allow PJM to cure 
the deficiency. 
The remaining four subjects, addressed in Sections III.B through III.E, concern 
implementation details that extend beyond the four corners of the instant filing: the separate 
settlement of battery injections and net-metered solar exports, multi-nodal aggregation 
geography, EDC registration readiness, and portfolio substitution rules. These issues bear 
directly on whether DERs can meaningfully participate in IRAS, but they are better addressed 
through a technical conference or coordinated follow-up proceeding rather than through

conditions imposed on this filing. Section III.F explains how the full set of requested reforms 
preserves reliability and avoids double counting. 
A. The Commission Should Ensure That Verified Peak Shaving Adjustments Reduce 
IRAS Exposure 
1. PJM’s Proposal Recognizes Approved PSA Values but Does Not Explain Their Effect 
on IRAS. PJM’s proposed Large Load Registry includes a field for a Peak Shaving 
Adjustment value under a qualifying state program. The registry does not itself create or 
approve that value. Under PJM’s existing PSA process, an authorized entity voluntarily 
submits a Peak Shaving Adjustment Plan, officer certification, and supporting state 
authorization for PJM review. PJM then approves a peak-shaving megawatt quantity by zone 
for inclusion in its load forecast. See PJM Manual 19: Load Forecasting and Analysis, 
Attachment D, at 39–43. The registry records the resulting PSA value. However, the IRAS 
proposal does not clearly explain how that value affects IRAS allocations. Because an 
approved PSA lowers forecast peak demand and the associated resource-adequacy need, 
excluding it from the IRAS calculation would overstate reliability risk and disregard verified 
load reductions. 
2. Virginia’s Enacted Framework Shows Qualifying State Programs Are Concrete and 
Measurable. Virginia SB 371 (identical to HB 284), 2026 Va. Acts chs. 377-378, codified at 
Va. Code § 56-596.7, became effective July 1, 2026. The statute defines demand flexibility 
and capacity-reduction credits and directs Dominion Energy Virginia and Appalachian Power 
Company to petition the Virginia State Corporation Commission by January 15, 2027 for 
voluntary demand-flexibility programs. Eligible measures include customer-sited storage, 
virtual power plants, demand response, efficiency, weatherization, heat pumps, and 
grid-enhancing technologies, with measured and verifiable results. The statute specifically

contemplates high-energy-demand customers funding or purchasing capacity-reduction 
credits from other retail customers. This legislation confirms that qualifying state programs 
are not hypothetical; they are enacted, scheduled, and designed to produce quantifiable 
peak-demand reductions. 
3. State-Recognized, Verified PSA Megawatts Should Offset IRAS Megawatts, Subject 
to Safeguards. The Commission should accept PJM’s filing only subject to a discrete 
clarification or compliance filing confirming that verified PSA megawatts reduce a Large 
Load’s IRAS obligation on a megawatt-for-megawatt basis. To protect reliability and prevent 
double counting, the offset should be subject to the following conditions: 
(a)​
Measurement and verification protocols consistent with the applicable 
qualifying state program; 
(b)​
Performance scoring that accounts for actual delivery during capacity shortage 
conditions; 
(c)​
Annual reconciliation of PSA values against observed load reductions; and 
(d)​
A prohibition on counting the same megawatt toward both a PSA offset and 
any other capacity resource obligation. 
B. A Workable IRAS DER Pathway Requires Separate Treatment of Battery Injections 
and Net-Metered Solar Exports 
If DER-backed capacity is to support IRAS compliance, PJM must establish 
settlement rules that distinguish battery storage injections from net-energy-metered solar 
exports. Without device-level submetering, a behind-the-meter battery that injects energy 
during a capacity event may be compensated twice: once through the customer’s retail NEM 
credit and again through wholesale capacity settlement. Conversely, requiring a customer to

forfeit NEM export compensation as a condition of wholesale capacity participation would 
deter enrollment and undermine the very DER pathway PJM purports to create. 
Other ISOs have addressed this problem. ISO-NE’s Forward Capacity Market Tariff 
section III.13.1.4 permits passive demand resources, including distributed generation 
measures, to hold capacity obligations without participating in wholesale energy or ancillary 
services markets. The Commission accepted ISO-NE’s Order 841 compliance filing requiring 
direct metering of behind-the-meter storage. ISO New England Inc., 169 FERC para. 61,140 
(2019), Docket No. ER19-470-000. ISO-NE’s Order 2222 compliance proceeding, Docket 
No. ER22-983, further developed device-level parallel metering and submetering 
configurations; the Commission accepted later compliance changes by delegated letter order 
in ER22-983-009, dated November 19, 2024, effective November 1, 2026. 
PJM’s own October 29, 2024 Regulation Market Only problem statement identifies a 
path for battery injections at NEM customer sites for ancillary services such as regulation, 
while acknowledging an implementation gap. That stakeholder process material confirms 
PJM recognizes the need for separate settlement but has not yet operationalized it for capacity 
purposes. 
The Commission should direct a technical conference or coordinated follow-up 
proceeding to develop device-level submetering protocols that settle battery injections 
independently from NEM-compensated solar exports, preserving retail NEM treatment while 
enabling wholesale capacity value without double compensation. 
C. Broader Multi-Nodal Aggregation Is Needed for Residential DERs to Support IRAS 
PJM’s current aggregation framework generally requires that distributed energy 
resources within a single aggregation be located at the same pricing node. A limited

multi-nodal exception exists, but it is capped at 167 MW across the entire RTO. These 
constraints present a structural barrier to residential-scale DER participation in IRAS. 
Residential solar-plus-storage systems are individually small, typically ranging from 5 to 25 
kW. To reach capacity levels meaningful for IRAS purposes, an aggregator must enroll 
hundreds or thousands of customers. Residential customers served by a single electric 
distribution company (“EDC”) are frequently spread across multiple pricing nodes. The 
single-node requirement forces aggregators to form numerous small, sub-scale aggregations 
rather than a single portfolio-level resource, increasing administrative burden and reducing 
the commercial viability of participation. The 167 MW RTO-wide multi-nodal cap, if fully 
subscribed by even a few aggregators, would foreclose additional residential participation 
entirely. 
Sunrun respectfully requests that the Commission, through a technical conference or 
coordinated follow-up proceeding, examine whether PJM should permit residential DER 
aggregations across an EDC service territory or, at minimum, across a transmission zone. 
Such geographic flexibility would allow residential portfolios to reach the scale necessary to 
provide meaningful capacity contributions under IRAS while remaining subject to 
appropriate distribution reliability limits. EDC-level or zonal aggregation is consistent with 
the Commission’s objectives in Order No. 2222, which directed RTOs to remove barriers to 
DER aggregation and recognized that overly narrow geographic constraints can impede 
participation. See Participation of Distributed Energy Res. Aggregations in Mkts. Operated 
by Reg’l Transmission Orgs. & Indep. Sys. Operators, Order No. 2222, 172 FERC para. 
61,247 (2020). Distribution reliability screening by the relevant EDC would remain in place, 
preserving the safety and operational review that PJM’s framework contemplates.

D. PJM Has Outlined Registration Timing, but State and EDC Readiness Requires 
Transparency and Accountability 
Sunrun does not ask the Commission to require PJM to create a registration process 
where none exists. PJM has already outlined a sequential process for DER aggregation 
registration in its 2026 Order 2222 compliance materials and the February 2, 2026 
Distributed Resources Subcommittee (“DISRS”) process materials. See PJM, 2222: 
Aggregate PNODE Creation, Distributed Resources Subcommittee (Sept. 1, 2026); PJM, 
DISRS Process Materials (Feb. 2, 2026). That process comprises three phases: (1) a 15-day 
location review; (2) a 15-day PJM and EDC data verification period; and (3) a 45-day EDC 
distribution reliability review. The 60-day EDC review window (phases two and three) is 
distinct from the full end-to-end processing timeline. Under this framework, PJM creates 
aggregate pricing nodes, while EDCs provide electrical location data, locational factors, and 
distribution reliability review. PJM has also stated that FERC declined to assert jurisdiction 
over DER interconnection, which remains governed by state and local processes. 
The primary implementation risk is uneven state and EDC readiness. Some EDCs 
may lack the staffing, data systems, or procedures to complete reviews within tariff deadlines, 
and state regulatory frameworks vary in their treatment of DER aggregation. A qualifying 
resource should not lose IRAS value solely because of administrative delay outside the 
aggregator’s control. At the same time, an overbroad deemed-approval mechanism could 
bypass legitimate distribution safety review. 
Sunrun respectfully requests that the Commission, through a technical conference or 
coordinated follow-up proceeding, address the following measures to ensure accountability: 
(e)​
Uniform data requirements for EDC submissions and aggregator applications 
across PJM.

(f)​
Transparent status tracking so that aggregators can monitor the progress of 
each registration phase. 
(g)​
A requirement that EDC denials be supported by reasoned, written 
explanations citing specific reliability concerns. 
(h)​
Adherence to tariff-specified deadlines, with periodic state and EDC readiness 
reporting to PJM and the Commission. 
(i)​
A mechanism, short of automatic deemed approval, that prevents qualifying 
resources from forfeiting IRAS value when delays are attributable to EDC or state 
administrative processes rather than substantive reliability concerns. 
E. Routine Additions and Like-for-Like Substitutions Should Not Restart Full Review 
or Be Barred Throughout a Delivery Year 
PJM’s March 9, 2026 DER Aggregator Participation Model materials state that 
modifications to a DER Capacity Aggregation Resource retrigger the full 60-day EDC review 
period and that inventory linked to such a resource may not be modified during the Delivery 
Year. PJM, DER Aggregator Participation Model (Mar. 9, 2026). These restrictions are 
incompatible with the operational reality of residential DER portfolios and, if applied to 
IRAS-linked commitments, will render those commitments unacceptably fragile. 
Residential solar-plus-storage portfolios experience ordinary customer turnover: 
customers move, cancel service, or replace equipment. A static-inventory requirement that 
freezes the composition of an aggregation for an entire Delivery Year ignores this reality. The 
aggregator’s performance obligation is measured at the portfolio level, not at the level of any 
individual device or customer. When a departing customer’s capacity is replaced by an 
equivalent resource at a comparable electrical location, the aggregate MW, the distribution

system impact, and the reliability contribution remain unchanged. Requiring a full 60-day 
review for such a substitution imposes delay disproportionate to any incremental reliability 
concern and creates a gap during which the aggregation may fall below its committed 
capacity. 
Sunrun requests that the Commission direct PJM to adopt expedited, ministerial 
treatment for routine additions and like-for-like substitutions that satisfy each of the 
following conditions: 
(j)​
The substitution or addition does not increase the aggregate committed MW of 
the DER Capacity Aggregation Resource. 
(k)​
The replacement resource does not materially change the relevant electrical 
location of the aggregation. 
(l)​
The change does not introduce a new distribution reliability concern as 
determined through targeted EDC screening. 
Under this framework, qualifying changes would proceed on a notice basis, with the 
EDC retaining authority to conduct a targeted screening rather than a full 60-day restart. 
Measurement, verification, and performance accountability would continue to apply at the 
aggregation level, preserving the Commission’s and PJM’s reliability objectives. This 
approach is consistent with the portfolio-level performance construct that PJM itself has 
adopted for DER aggregations and prevents qualifying resources from losing IRAS value due 
to routine portfolio management. 
F. These Reforms Preserve Reliability and Avoid Double Counting While Making 
PJM’s Stated DER Pathway Usable

The clarifications and process reforms described in Sections III.A through III.E are 
consistent with PJM’s stated reliability objectives and with the Commission’s directives in 
Orders 2222 and 841. Each request is designed to complete PJM’s own DER pathway, not to 
rewrite the Interim Resource Adequacy Service proposal. 
The safeguards Sunrun proposes operate in concert to protect reliability and prevent 
double counting: 
(m)​
Measurement and Verification: PSA offsets and DER capacity contributions 
would be validated through defined protocols before any IRAS obligation is reduced, 
ensuring that only demonstrated load reductions receive credit. 
(n)​
Performance Scoring: Aggregation-level performance obligations hold DER 
providers accountable for delivery during capacity shortage emergencies, consistent 
with PJM’s existing performance assessment framework. 
(o)​
Reconciliation: Post-delivery-year reconciliation would true up any 
discrepancy between credited capacity and actual performance, preserving the 
integrity of resource adequacy accounting. 
(p)​
No-Double-Counting Provisions: Device-level submetering of battery 
injections, separate from NEM-compensated solar exports, prevents the same 
megawatt-hour from receiving both retail net-metering compensation and wholesale 
capacity or energy credit. PSA megawatts credited against IRAS obligations would be 
excluded from any other capacity supply commitment. 
(q)​
Distribution Reliability Screening: Targeted EDC review for routine 
substitutions and additions, rather than full 60-day restarts, preserves the EDC’s 
authority to identify and address legitimate safety and reliability concerns while 
removing unnecessary administrative barriers.

Taken together, these safeguards ensure that PJM’s resource adequacy framework 
accounts for verified DER contributions without compromising system reliability. The 
Commission can accept PJM’s filing subject to a discrete compliance filing on PSA 
treatment, confident that the broader DER implementation issues identified here are 
appropriate subjects for a technical conference or coordinated follow-up proceeding. 
IV. Conclusion and Prayer for Relief 
For the reasons set forth above, Sunrun Inc. respectfully requests that the Commission: 
(r)​
Grant Sunrun’s motion to intervene in Docket No. ER26-3515-000; 
(s)​
Accept PJM’s August 13, 2026 filing, Accession No. 20260813-5118, subject 
to a discrete clarification or compliance filing confirming that verified Peak Shaving 
Adjustment values under qualifying state programs reduce a Large Load’s IRAS 
obligations on a megawatt-for-megawatt basis, with appropriate measurement and 
verification, performance scoring, reconciliation, and no-double-counting safeguards; 
or, in the alternative, reject the filing without prejudice to allow PJM to refile with 
such provisions; 
(t)​
Convene a technical conference or direct a coordinated follow-up proceeding 
to address: (a) separate settlement of battery storage injections and net-metered solar 
exports through device-level submetering; (b) broader multi-nodal aggregation rules 
permitting residential DERs to aggregate across an electric distribution company 
service territory or transmission zone; (c) uniform data requirements, transparent 
status tracking, reasoned denials, tariff-deadline adherence, and state and EDC 
readiness reporting for DER registration, including a mechanism to prevent qualifying 
resources from losing IRAS value solely because of administrative delay; and (d)

expedited, ministerial treatment for like-for-like substitutions and routine additions to 
DER aggregation portfolios that do not increase aggregate MW, materially change the 
relevant electrical location, or create new distribution reliability concerns; and 
(u)​
Grant such other and further relief as the Commission deems just and 
appropriate. 
Respectfully submitted, 
/s/ S. Becca Smith
